name: Maya mercury-lead-arsenic red pigment

lead: The ancient Maya used red mineral pigments to colour bodies, burials, pottery and temple walls. Analyses of painted bones from Maya sites identify red ochre (hematite) and cinnabar (mercury sulfide) as the main pigments, mixed with organic binders. Cinnabar is described as the pigment of elite ritual, hematite as the more widely available one.

The vivid colour is the appearance payoff: the 7th-century Red Queen of Palenque was covered in bright red cinnabar powder. A 2021 study of funerary pigments from Xcambo found beeswax and pine resin among the binders [1][2]. Mercury is toxic, and researchers have also discussed environmental contamination from Maya cinnabar use.

paras: Pigment was applied as a powder or paste, bound with ingredients such as beeswax and resin, in funerary rites and on objects and architecture [1]. It is a historical practice documented from archaeology rather than a product in current use.

Cinnabar is mercury sulfide, and its mercury content is the source of its toxicity; ancient Romans recognised hazards to those who mined and processed it [2]. Researchers have reported mercury in Maya lake sediments linked to pigment use.

angle.text: The Maya applied red mineral pigments to bodies and burials for vivid ritual colouring. This is a historical practice documented in archaeology, not a current cosmetic.

lead: Maya red pigments were mineral colours used on the bodies of the dead, on pottery and on buildings. Studies of painted human remains from Maya sites identify cinnabar (mercury sulfide) and red ochre or hematite (iron oxide) as the main red pigments, with cinnabar associated with elite rituals and hematite with wider use [1].

The effect was a bright scarlet. In the 7th-century tomb of the Red Queen at Palenque, the remains of a noblewoman and the objects in her sarcophagus were covered with cinnabar powder [2]. Use of cinnabar in the New World is described as beginning with the Olmec [2].

A 2021 study in Molecules used proton NMR to analyse organic components in pre-Hispanic Mayan funerary pigments from Xcambo, identifying beeswax as a base and binder and abietane (pine) resin as an aromatic, binding component; copal found in elite pigments was absent from those samples [1]. The sources consulted report cinnabar and hematite as the colourants and do not report lead or arsenic.

paras: Funerary and ritual red among the Maya was produced chiefly from cinnabar and hematite. Earlier diffraction and microscopy studies found mainly inorganic minerals in these pigments, and the 2021 NMR study focused on the organic binders [1].

Pigments were applied to painted bones, burials, ceramics and architecture. Examples include the Red Queen's tomb at Palenque [2], and analyses of painted remains at Xcambo [1]. Cinnabar use elsewhere ranges from Roman wall paint and cosmetics to burials in Spain and mummy clothing in Chile [2].
Cinnabar is a mercury compound; its toxicity was recognised by the Romans, and miners at Almaden were exposed to mercury fumes [2].
No studies found. The related research is archaeological chemistry rather than clinical: a 2021 NMR analysis of Xcambo funerary pigments [1].
